title: Results Section-Audit Map
subject: optimality, runtime, and deployment claims
eyebrow: Generic IEEE/ACM engineering conventions · synthetic Results excerpt
summary: Three findings map the excerpt's load-bearing claims to the supplied solver-log evidence. The map distinguishes exact global optimality from solver status under a relative MIP-gap tolerance, wall-clock guarantees from incomplete solver-log timing, and finite offline optimization evidence from real-time deployment readiness.
footer: Generated on 3 August 2026 from the supplied synthetic excerpt by applying the repository-local ieee-acm-paper-writing skill. No target publication was supplied, so venue-specific compliance was not exercised. The HTML presents the canonical text audit and adds no finding or conclusion.

findings.title: Universal exact-optimality claim is contradicted
findings.source: The optimizer always returns the global optimum
findings.evidence: The solver logs show that only 9 of 12 runs ended with status OPTIMAL under a 1% relative MIP-gap tolerance. The other 3 reached the time limit with feasible incumbents and final gaps of 4.1%, 5.3%, and 7.8%. No exact-optimality certificate is supplied.
findings.consequence: The universal guarantee is false for the reported evaluation set, and the 9 tolerance-based solver statuses do not establish exact global optimality without an applicable exact certificate.
findings.correction: Remove the guarantee. Report the observed statuses and tolerance: 9 of 12 runs ended with solver status OPTIMAL under the 1% relative MIP-gap tolerance; 3 timed out with feasible incumbents at final gaps of 4.1%, 5.3%, and 7.8%.

findings.title: Ten-second runtime guarantee is contradicted and unmeasured
findings.evidence: Three runs reached the 60 s time limit, directly contradicting the claim for the complete 12-instance set. No per-run timing measurements outside the solver logs are supplied, so the 10 s bound is also unsupported for the 9 remaining runs.
findings.consequence: The excerpt states a deterministic wall-clock bound that the supplied evidence disproves for at least 3 runs and does not verify for the others.
findings.correction: Delete the 10 s claim. If runtime is to be reported, supply per-instance wall-clock measurements with the measurement method, hardware, solver version and settings, thread count, and aggregation; retain the three 60 s timeouts in the reported distribution.

findings.title: Real-time deployment readiness is unsupported
findings.source: The method is therefore ready for real-time deployment.
findings.evidence: No deployment experiment is supplied. Solver logs from 12 instances, including three 60 s timeouts, do not establish an operational deadline, end-to-end latency, tail behavior, jitter, scheduling effects, hardware suitability, integration overhead, deadline-miss consequences, or safety under deployment conditions.
findings.consequence: The conclusion crosses from bounded offline solver behavior to system-level real-time and deployment readiness without an evaluated bridge.
findings.correction: Remove the deployment-readiness conclusion. State only the finite solver outcomes. A future readiness claim requires a defined operational deadline and representative end-to-end deployment measurements, including latency distributions and deadline misses, on the intended hardware and workload.
